name: Deepdale
description: Deepdale is the oldest continuously used professional football stadium in the world. Originally Deepdale Farm, leased in 1875. First football match played October 5, 1878. Preston North End achieved the 'Double' (league and FA Cup) in the inaugural 1888-89 season.

name: Wellington Road
description: Wellington Road was Aston Villa's home from 1876 to 1897. Initially lacked spectator facilities, with players changing in a nearby blacksmith's shed. Hosted record crowd of 26,849 for FA Cup match against Preston North End in January 1888. First league match was September 15, 1888, Villa defeating Stoke 5-1.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md on ws/H-02-grounds): 26,849 (Ultimate Directory) is the record crowd for the FA Cup tie with Preston on 7 Jan 1888, estimated at 20,000 to 30,000 by AVDB, when the crowd overran the ground; it is not a capacity. Capacity set to 20,000 (game estimate: the low end of that crowd).

name: Dudley Road
description: Wolves played at Dudley Road from 1881 to 1889. First Football League match was September 8, 1888, a 1-1 draw against Aston Villa. Record attendance was 10,000 for FA Cup match against The Wednesday in March 1889. Wolves moved to Molineux in 1889.

name: Ewood Park
description: Ewood Park (originally Ewood Bridge) opened in April 1882 as a multi-purpose sports venue. Blackburn Rovers played several matches there in 1882 before moving in permanently in 1890. Featured horse boxes, dressing tents, refreshment saloon, lavatories, and a grandstand. Club purchased the freehold in 1893 for £2,500.

name: Leamington Road
description: Blackburn Rovers' home from 1881 to 1890, before Ewood Park. Highest League crowd 15,000 v Preston North End on 2 November 1889. Built over with housing after 1890.
notes: Capacity set to the record crowd; value, landValue and annualRent are game estimates (not sourced), in line with the other grounds of the period.

name: Pike's Lane
description: Pike's Lane was Bolton Wanderers' home from 1880 until 1895. Featured embankments on both sides, later a grandstand and wooden terracing. On September 8, 1888, hosted one of the inaugural Football League matches, with Kenny Davenport scoring the first-ever Football League goal. Often criticized for poor pitch conditions.

name: Stoney Lane
description: Stoney Lane served as West Bromwich Albion's home from 1885 to 1900. Secured a seven-year lease for £28 per annum from local undertaker Mr. H. Webb. Featured a wooden grandstand known as 'Noah's Ark' accommodating 600 spectators. First league match was September 29, 1888, Albion defeating Burnley 4-3.

name: Thorneyholme Road
description: Thorneyholme Road was shared by Accrington Cricket Club (since 1877) and Accrington Football Club (founded 1878, known as 'Owd Reds'). The football pitch was at the western end, featuring a covered stand and uncovered seating. First league match was October 6, 1888, a 4-4 draw against Wolverhampton Wanderers.

name: Anfield
description: Everton moved to Anfield in 1884, ground owned by John Orrell. In 1885, John Houlding purchased Anfield for approximately £6,000. Rent increased from £100 (1888) to £240 (1891), causing tensions. Everton left Anfield in 1892 to move to Goodison Park. Houlding then founded Liverpool FC to occupy the vacant Anfield.

name: Turf Moor
description: Turf Moor has been associated with sports since at least 1843 when Burnley Cricket Club relocated there. In 1883, the cricket club invited Burnley FC to move from Calder Vale. In 1885, constructed an 800-seat wooden grandstand and uncovered standing for 5,000. First league match was October 6, 1888, Burnley defeating Bolton Wanderers 4-1.

name: Racecourse Ground
description: The County Cricket Ground inside the southern curve of Derby Racecourse, off Nottingham Road. Derby County played across its west end from 27 September 1884 to 1895, with the large racecourse grandstand and a cricket and football pavilion built in 1885. It staged the 1886 FA Cup final replay (15,000), the first final outside London. Race meetings came first, which drove the club to the Baseball Ground in 1895.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md on ws/H-02-grounds; docs/data/history/clubs/derby-county.md): the old description told the Baseball Ground's story; replaced with the County Ground's.

name: Trent Bridge
description: Notts County, established in 1862 (world's oldest professional football club), began playing at Trent Bridge in 1883, a venue primarily known for cricket. First home Football League match was October 6, 1888, drawing 3-3 against Blackburn Rovers. Shared use with cricket club presented challenges. Won FA Cup in 1894.

name: Victoria Ground
description: The Victoria Ground served as Stoke's home from 1878 until 1997, marking 119 years of football history. At the time of its demolition, it was the oldest operational ground in the Football League. First league match was September 8, 1888, a 2-0 defeat against West Bromwich Albion.

name: Vincent Square
description: Vincent Square is a grass-covered square in Westminster, London. It is the playing field of Westminster School and was the home ground of the Old Westminsters.

name: Dolphin Ground
description: The Dolphin Ground in Slough was the home ground of the Swifts, a prominent amateur club in the early days of English football.

name: Brighton College Grounds
description: The playing fields of Brighton College, used by the Old Brightonians amateur team.

name: Racecourse Ground
description: The Racecourse Ground is the oldest international football stadium in the world that still hosts international matches. Home of Wrexham since their formation.

name: Gregory Ground
description: The Gregory Ground in Lenton was Nottingham Forest's home from 1882 to 1890 before moving to the Town Ground.

name: Ulsterville Avenue
description: Linfield's second home ground, from 1889, after the Meadow.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/linfield.md): Linfield moved here in 1889 (in 1888-89 they were at the Meadow, `the-meadow-belfast`); was opened 1886.

name: The Meadow
description: Linfield Athletic's first ground, a field behind the mill in Belfast, used until the move to Ulsterville Avenue in 1889.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/linfield.md): Linfield's 1888-89 ground. Opened = the club's founding year (1886); capacity and value, landValue and annualRent are game estimates (not sourced), copied from the ground this season used before H-01b (`ulsterville-avenue`).

name: Archway Ground
description: The original home of Witton Albion in Northwich.

name: Redlam Brow
description: Witton F.C. (Blackburn) played at Redlam Brow by 1881; bigger matches were sometimes at Witton Park.
notes: Opening year and capacity not found; capacity, value, landValue and annualRent are game estimates.

name: Hawthorne Road
description: Hawthorne Road was the home of the original Bootle FC, who were rivals to Everton in the early years of Merseyside football.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/bootle.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md): Bootle's football use from 1884 per the ground article (1883 per the club article); was 1880.

name: Maidstone Road Ground
description: Chatham's enclosed ground from 1889, after the FA required gate-taking grounds.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/chatham-town.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md): Chatham moved here in 1889 and enclosed it with a seated pavilion for GBP 125 (in 1888-89 they played on the Lines, `great-lines`); was opened 1882.

name: The Lines
description: Army-owned open ground at Chatham (the Great Lines), used by Chatham until 1889. Unfenced: Army rules meant no admission could be charged. The 17,000 at the 1889 FA Cup tie with West Bromwich Albion can only be an estimate.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/chatham-town.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md on ws/H-02-grounds): Chatham's 1888-89 ground; moved to Maidstone Road in 1889 after the FA required enclosed grounds. No gate could be taken here; the model has no 'no admission' flag, so capacity is copied from `maidstone-road-ground` and annualRent is 0 (Army land); value and landValue are game estimates. Opened year not found.

name: South Shore Ground
description: The home ground of South Shore FC in Blackpool, who later merged with Blackpool St John's to form Blackpool FC.

name: Abbey Park
description: Abbey Park was the home of Grimsby Town from 1889 to 1899. It was one of the better equipped non-league grounds of the era.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/grimsby-town.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md): first match 30 Aug 1889 (was opened 1880, Clee Park's year); Grimsby's ground from 1889-90.

name: Clee Park
description: Grimsby Town's ground from 1880 to the summer of 1889, with a grandstand and a 300-seat stand that were moved to Abbey Park in 1889. Preston North End came here for the FA Cup on 16 February 1889 before about 8,000.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/grimsby-town.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md on ws/H-02-grounds): Grimsby's 1888-89 ground (Abbey Park's first match was 30 Aug 1889). Capacity = the 1889 FA Cup crowd (exact capacity not found); value, landValue and annualRent are game estimates (not sourced), copied from the ground this season used before H-01b (`abbey-park`).

name: Blue House Field
description: Sunderland Albion's first home ground in Hendon, Sunderland.

name: Halliwell Road Ground
description: The home ground of Halliwell FC in Bolton, rivals to Bolton Wanderers.

name: Alexandra Recreation Ground
description: Crewe Alexandra's home ground from 1877 to 1898, located near the railway station.

name: Charterhouse School Grounds
description: The playing fields of Charterhouse School in Godalming, home of the Old Carthusians.

name: Derby Junction Ground
description: The home ground of Derby Junction, one of the prominent clubs in Derby before the rise of Derby County.

name: Castle Ground
description: The Castle Ground in the Meadows, Nottingham: Notts Rangers' ground by 1884 until September 1886, and Notts County's second ground. Not the later Castle Cricket Ground by Trent Bridge.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/notts-rangers.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md): Notts Rangers left it for Meadow Lane in Sep 1886 (`meadow-lane` is their 1888-89 ground); Notts County used it as a second ground.

name: Meadow Lane
description: Notts Rangers' ground from September 1886, after the Castle Ground.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/notts-rangers.md; docs/data/history/GROUNDS_1888-89.md on ws/H-02-grounds): Notts Rangers moved here in Sep 1886 (Athletic News per H-02). Whether it is the site of Notts County's later Meadow Lane (1910) is not confirmed. Capacity and value, landValue and annualRent are game estimates (not sourced), copied from the ground this season used before H-01b (`castle-ground`).

name: Olive Grove
description: Olive Grove was the home of Sheffield Wednesday from 1887 to 1899. It hosted the first ever Steel City Derby.

name: Cape Hill
description: Cape Hill was the home of Birmingham St George's, located near the Mitchells & Butlers brewery.

name: Recreation Ground
description: The home ground of Long Eaton Rangers in Derbyshire.

name: Muntz Street
description: Muntz Street, also known as Coventry Road, was the home of Small Heath (later Birmingham City) from 1877 to 1906.

name: Chuckery Ground
description: The Chuckery Ground was the first home of the newly merged Walsall Town Swifts.
notes: H-01b (docs/data/history/clubs/walsall.md): used by both parent clubs (Walsall Town, Walsall Swifts) since April 1881; was 1888 (the merger year).

name: Heeley Ground
description: The home ground of Heeley FC, one of the oldest clubs in Sheffield.
